source: Somsak Wannasaree, "Banana Orchards" (Khmer translation, 1997), section 7 (planting and spacing)
text:
Recommended spacing varies considerably depending on why the banana is being planted, not just which variety is used:

- Dwarf/small varieties grown as the main crop: about 3 x 3m spacing.
- Vigorous, large-statured varieties grown as a long-term main crop: spacing can go as wide as 10 x 10m.
- Banana grown as shade/support alongside other tree crops in a mixed planting: about 8 x 8m, wide enough to leave room for the companion trees.
- Banana grown mainly as a short-term nurse crop to provide shade for young perennial tree seedlings (for example, while establishing a new fruit orchard) before being removed once the main trees are established: much tighter spacing, around 2 x 3m, is acceptable since these plants are temporary.
- Banana grown as a fast-turnover cash crop where longevity of the planting matters less than getting an early return: closer spacing such as 5 x 5m is workable.

The underlying principle is a trade-off between planting density and how long the stand needs to remain productive: closer spacing gives more plants and earlier income per unit area but shortens the productive life of the planting and increases competition between clumps over time, while wider spacing supports each clump better for a longer productive run at plantation scale.
